# Four Quadrants, and What They Are Not {#sec-fourth-quadrant}

In 2009, the *International Journal of Forecasting* published a paper with a title that sounds like
a technical correction and is not one: "Errors, Robustness, and the Fourth Quadrant"
[@taleb2009]. It appeared in volume 25, issue 4, pages 744 to 759, in print in October 2009 and
online that August, and OpenAlex records 96 citations for it while Semantic Scholar records 86.
Both figures are given because they differ and neither is authoritative. Databases disagree. This is normal.

I begin Part II with this paper because it marks the transition the part is about. Part I described
what the world is like. This paper asks what follows for the way you decide, and its answer takes
the form of a map rather than a prescription.

The map has four cells, and almost every discussion of the paper gets the axes wrong. So this
chapter spends most of its length on what the axes are, then a short section on what the paper
claims follows from them, and a final section on what the paper does not claim — which is more than
readers generally assume.

## The two axes

The first axis is the **probability structure**: whether the relevant uncertainty lives in a
thin-tailed world or a fat-tailed one. These are the Mediocristan and Extremistan of the author's
earlier work, and the distinction is the same one Part I spent six chapters establishing.

The second axis is the **decision structure**, and it is the part that gets misreported. The
question is not how large or how important the decision is. It is whether the decision depends
only on whether an event occurs, or also on how much is at stake when it does.

Some decisions are of the first kind. Did the patient have the disease? Is the bridge within its
load rating? The action follows from the answer, and the magnitude of the outcome is fixed by the
protocol. Call these M0 decisions, using the paper's notation.

Other decisions are of the second kind. A portfolio position, an insurance contract, a bet on an
election with a payoff proportional to the margin: here the size of the outcome varies across
realizations, and the decision depends on properties of the distribution beyond the probability of
an event.

**The distinction is not about complexity or importance. It is about whether the payoff magnitude enters the decision.** It is about magnitudes. A trivial financial position is M1 because the amount matters. A grave
medical decision can be M0 because the treatment is the same regardless of severity.

| | Thin-tailed | Fat-tailed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Binary decision (M0)** | The domain of textbook statistics: casinos, controlled trials, quality control | Known to be difficult; rare in practice, because fat-tailed phenomena seldom present as binary questions |
| **Payoff-dependent decision (M1+)** | Statistics performs well, by the paper's own account | The fourth quadrant: the paper's claim is that statistically based claims should not carry decisions here |

## The two errors in reading this table

**Error one: treating the cells as risk levels.** The quadrants are not ordered from safe to
dangerous. A fat-tailed M0 decision is not more dangerous than a thin-tailed M1 decision; the two
differ in which tools apply. A reader who sorts the cells by risk has lost the framework and kept
the diagram.

**Error two: collapsing the axes.** Most citations of this paper compress it into "there are
predictable and unpredictable things." That loses the second axis entirely, and the second axis is
the paper's contribution. **The insight is that fat tails alone do not disable statistical
reasoning. Fat tails combined with payoff dependence do.**

## The casino

The paper's most quoted example is the casino, and its role is worth stating precisely because it
is usually reduced to a quip.

A casino is a thin-tailed, M0 environment. The rules fix the payoffs, the probabilities are
designed rather than estimated, the decision is whether to play a game with a known edge, and the
outcome magnitude is bounded per round by the table limit.

**Nothing in a casino requires a judgement about the world.** The probabilities are properties of
the equipment. When a casino estimates, it estimates mechanical drift, not the shape of
uncertainty.

The error the paper names — the ludic fallacy — is the transfer of this situation's properties to
situations that lack them. Its specific failure is that it makes estimation look easier than it is:
in a designed game, the model is given; in everything else, the model is a guess that has been
dressed up as a measurement.

## What the paper actually claims

Compressed to its argument, and stated in the book's vocabulary from Chapter 26.

**A grade II claim.** That there exists a class of problems — fat-tailed, payoff-dependent — in
which the reliability of statistical inference is structurally lower than in the others. The claim
is qualitative. It does not name a threshold, a family, or a parameter.

**A construction.** The two-by-two map itself, which is a taxonomy rather than a finding.

**A set of behavioural rules**, offered in the same paper and in its longer public version: avoid
optimisation; avoid forecasting remote payoffs; be careful with scenario analysis and stress
tests, because the scenarios are chosen by the analyst; watch for horizon mismatches; beware moral
hazard; do not use variance-like measures for risk; do not read low volatility as low risk.

Those rules are the paper's most useful output and the least quantitative part of it. They require
no parameters, which is the point: **in the fourth quadrant, a rule that requires no estimate is
worth more than a model that requires several.**

## What the paper is not

Three corrections, each documented rather than asserted.

**It is not a discussion paper.** The journal does publish that format, complete with commentaries
and rejoinders, and it did so in the same era. A search of the journal's records for 2009 and 2010
turns up no commentary or reply attached to this paper. It appeared as part of a special section on
low predictability, alongside work by other authors on forecasting under low signal [@taleb2009].
I checked this because I had assumed otherwise, and the record says no.

**It does not claim that statistics is useless.** The table above gives the paper's own verdict on
the thin-tailed, payoff-dependent cell: statistical methods perform well there. The target is the
cell, not the discipline.

**It does not contain the phrase that is most often attributed to it.** The argument is frequently
summarised as "in the fourth quadrant, model error dominates estimation error." That formulation is
consistent with the paper's argument and appears in the author's public exposition of it, but I
could not verify it in the published text, which was not available to me. The chapter therefore
does not put it in quotation marks.

## Using the map

A practical procedure, in three questions.

**Question one: is the payoff bounded?** What is the worst outcome of being wrong, in units that
matter to the decision-maker? If the answer is a fixed, survivable amount, the decision has M0-like
properties. If it scales with the realization, it does not.

**Question two: which tail?** Is the relevant uncertainty thin-tailed — a mechanism with bounded
outcomes and many independent contributors — or fat-tailed? Part I's tests apply here.

**Question three: what tool survives the cell?** In the thin-tailed payoff-dependent cell, ordinary
estimation. In the fat-tailed binary cell, rare in practice, ordinary estimation with warnings. In
the fat-tailed payoff-dependent cell, the rules above, which avoid estimating anything.

The procedure is short and its difficulty is in question two, which is the hard question of Part I
wearing different clothes. **The map does not solve the estimation problem. It tells you when the
estimation problem is not the binding constraint.**

## Claim and tool

The claim: that the applicability of statistical inference depends jointly on tail behaviour and on
payoff structure, so that either alone is an incomplete diagnostic.

The tool: the map, and the behavioural rules that come with it.

Graded by the book's vocabulary, the tool is a **grade II construction**. Its qualitative content —
cells differ in which tools apply — survives changes of domain, from markets to medicine to
infrastructure. Its specific calibration does not: what counts as a payoff-dependent decision is a
judgement, and honest practitioners will disagree at the margins.

## Boundary conditions

The map presumes that the two questions can be answered. Where the payoff structure is unclear or
the tail behaviour cannot be characterised, the classification is unavailable, and a procedure that
requires classification cannot be started.

It presumes stationary-enough tails that "fat-tailed" is a stable description, which the previous
chapters showed to be a strong presumption.

And it does not tell you what to do beyond the avoidance rules. The map identifies where the
standard toolkit does not apply. Filling the gap — with precaution, with convexity, with structure
that bounds losses — occupies the rest of Part II.

## What the quadrants do not say about magnitude

The map classifies situations. It does not measure them, and the temptation to read a severity
ranking into it should be resisted explicitly.

**The cells are not ordered by danger.** A problem in the second quadrant — thin tailed, payoff
dependent — can be more consequential in absolute terms than a small fourth-quadrant exposure. A
reliable model of a large but bounded risk is a manageable object; the concern in the fourth quadrant
is the reliability of the method, not the size of the stakes.

**The axes are qualitative in the paper's own presentation.** Systemic-or-not and
magnitude-dependent-or-not are judgements about structure, not measurements. There is no threshold
count that separates the cells, which is why the assignment is arguable and why the book treats it as
a decision to be stated rather than a classification to be computed.

**The boundary cases are where the work is.** A risk that is local in one dimension and systemic in
another — a chemical spill contained by a site boundary but transported by water — sits between
cells, and the useful output in such a case is a statement of which property is doing the work.

**What the map is for.** It is a first-pass filter, applied before any model is chosen, whose value
lies in the cases it excludes from ordinary treatment. Used that way it takes minutes. Used as a
taxonomy to be completed for its own sake, it becomes paperwork, which is the failure mode the
instrument chapter catalogues.

## Applying the map in five minutes

A practical procedure for the classification, since the value of the map is in the speed with which it
excludes the ordinary cases.

**Minute one. Name the event.** What is the outcome being reasoned about. Vague events produce vague
classifications.

**Minute two. Ask whether magnitude enters the outcome.** If the decision is the same whatever the size
of the event, the exposure is M0 and the second axis falls away.

**Minute three. Ask whether failure propagates.** Does the loss stay where it happened, or move through
a network of counterparties, systems or populations. **Local is the common answer and the one that most
often goes unchecked.**

**Minute four. Assign the cell and say which one.** Out loud, or on paper. The statement is the output.

**Minute five. Say what the cell excludes.** If the cell is one of the three ordinary ones, the correct
response is the standard apparatus, and the map's contribution is the permission to use it without
further agonising.

**Why five minutes is the right budget.** A classification that takes an hour will not be done, and the
cases where the classification is genuinely difficult are the ones where the difficulty is the finding.
**Where the five minutes end without a cell, the disagreement about the cell is the deliverable.**

**What to record.** The event, the two answers, the cell, and the date. Six months later, the record is
the only thing that shows whether the classification was reasonable or convenient.

## The quadrants and the precautionary principle

Two devices in this book are drawn from the same source and they are related in a way worth making explicit,
because readers often carry one without the other.

**The relation.** A problem in the fourth quadrant — fat-tailed, payoff-dependent — is a problem where the
standard apparatus fails. A problem that is also systemic is a problem where the failure propagates. **The
precautionary principle is the decision rule for the intersection: fourth quadrant plus systemic exposure.**

**What each contributes.**

**The quadrant map tells you that the method is inapplicable.** It is diagnostic, and it says nothing about
what to do.

**The precaution criterion tells you what to do.** It applies where the exposure is systemic and the
distribution fat-tailed, and it prescribes a burden shift and, in practice, a bounding move.

**Why the two are often separated in the literature.** The quadrant paper is about statistical practice and
the precaution paper is about policy. **The separation is disciplinary rather than logical, and a reader who
has both finds that each answers the question the other raises.**

**Three cases that clarify the relation.**

**A local fat-tailed risk.** Fourth quadrant, not systemic. **The map says the standard method fails; the
criterion says the principle does not apply and ordinary analysis resumes.** This is the case most often
confused, and it is where the precautionary rule's negative half does its work.

**A systemic thin-tailed risk.** Precaution does not apply, and the ordinary apparatus handles it. **Rare in
practice and worth noting because it shows that systemic exposure alone is not sufficient.**

**A systemic fat-tailed risk.** Both apply. **This is the small intersection the two devices were built
for, and it is smaller than the rhetoric around either suggests.**

## The quadrants and the size of the bet

The map classifies situations and says nothing about sizing. The connection between the two is worth stating,
because the map is often used to justify a position size and the justification does not follow.

**What the map does not give.** A magnitude, a probability, a fraction. **A fourth-quadrant classification
says the standard apparatus does not apply; it does not say how much to stake.**

**What follows from the cell. Three different sizing contexts.**

**First and third quadrants.** Ordinary sizing applies, with the discount for estimation error. **The map's
contribution is permission to use the standard machinery.**

**Second quadrant.** Ordinary sizing applies and the risk management must be strict, because the payoff
dependence means the position's value moves with an outcome whose size is not bounded by the position.

**Fourth quadrant.** The sizing machinery requires the quantities to exist. **Where they do not, sizing is
replaced by a bound; where they exist and cannot be estimated, by a bound with a rule. This is the grid's
contribution, and it is a different device from the map.**

**What the distinction prevents.** Two errors. **Sizing a fourth-quadrant exposure from an estimated mean that
may not exist**, which produces a confident fraction from a non-existent quantity. And **refusing to size
anything in the fourth quadrant**, which abandons the positions where a bounded structure is available.

**Why the two devices are kept separate.** The map is about which method applies; the grid is about which
output is available; the sizing rules are about how much. **Three questions, three devices, and the common
error is to use the first to answer the third.**

## The four cells as four kinds of argument

Each cell implies a different form of argument, and the forms are what a practitioner actually produces when
arguing for a decision. Naming them makes the map usable in a meeting.

**First cell. Thin tailed, magnitude-independent.** The argument is a calculation. **Cost-benefit, expected
value, a discounted comparison. The cell licenses the ordinary apparatus, and the argument's form is
arithmetic.**

**Second cell. Thin tailed, magnitude-dependent.** The argument is a comparison of exposures. **Concentration,
limits, correlation. The form is structural, and the numbers involved are the position's size and the
exposure's bound.**

**Third cell. Fat tailed, magnitude-independent.** The argument is about frequency and shape. **How often, at
what level, with what uncertainty. The form is empirical, and it is the cell where the tail comparison of
Chapter 1 belongs.**

**Fourth cell. Fat tailed, magnitude-dependent.** The argument cannot be a calculation. **It is a screening
argument: which exposures are irreversible, which can be bounded, and what scale is available. The form is
structural, and the numbers, if any, are bounds.**

**What the naming achieves. Three things.**

**It tells a practitioner what kind of memo to write.** A fourth-cell decision argued in first-cell form is a
category error, and the error is common.

**It tells a reviewer what to look for.** In the fourth cell, an expected value is a sign that the argument's
form does not match its cell.

**It explains why the cells feel different.** They are not four points on a scale; they are four argument
forms, and moving between them changes what counts as evidence.

**Why the map is worth its five minutes for this reason alone.** Because the most common analytical failure in
this book's material is a fourth-cell problem argued with first-cell tools, and naming the form makes the
mismatch visible before the analysis is finished.

## The map and the second opinion

The classification is a judgement, and judgements benefit from being made twice. The map's structure makes the
second opinion cheap, and this section states how to run it.

**What a second classifier is given. Three items.**

**The event.** Not the decision, the event being reasoned about.

**The two questions.** Whether magnitude enters the outcome, and whether failure propagates. **Stated as
questions rather than as criteria, so that the second classifier answers rather than confirms.**

**No cell.** The first classifier's cell is withheld. **Which is the whole of the method: a second opinion that
sees the first one's answer is a ratification.**

**What disagreements mean. Three kinds.**

**Disagreement about the event.** The two classifiers were reasoning about different things. **The most common
disagreement and the most informative, because it reveals that the decision has not been specified.**

**Disagreement about propagation.** One sees a network where the other sees a boundary. **The substantive case,
and the one that reveals where the analysis's assumptions live.**

**Disagreement about magnitude dependence.** Usually a disagreement about whether a quantity matters, which is a
question about the decision rather than about the world. **The answer is to state the decision more precisely.**

**What to record.** The two cells, the disagreement if any, and the date. **A cell agreed between two classifiers
is not evidence that it is right; it is evidence that it is not idiosyncratic, which is the property that makes
it usable in a group.**

**Why the second opinion is worth the ten minutes.** Because the map's errors are systematic in one direction:
the local-and-mild cell is easier to assign than the systemic-and-severe one, and a single classifier working
alone has no mechanism for noticing that the assignment was the convenient one. **Two answers, one of them taken
without seeing the other, is the cheapest available correction.**

## The map and the ordinary decision

The four cells are presented for problems with stakes. Their most frequent application is to ordinary decisions
whose cells are obvious, and the value there is a reduction in unnecessary analysis.

**The ordinary case. One example.** A firm decides whether to renew a software licence. **Thin tailed, no
magnitude dependence, local exposure. First cell. Ordinary analysis.**

**What the map contributes here. One thing.** Permission. **The analysis does not need to be agnostic, robust, or
scenario-based, and the map's contribution to this decision is that the standard toolkit is the right one.**

**Why that contribution matters. Three reasons.**

**It removes the temptation to apply the apparatus where it is not needed.** Which is a real cost in
organisations that have adopted a framework.

**It makes the framework's recommendations credible where the cell is serious.** An apparatus that says yes
sometimes is one whose no means something.

**It reduces the number of decisions receiving elaborate treatment.** Which is where the analysis budget actually
goes.

**What the map does not do for an ordinary decision. Anything else.** No estimate, no range, no structural
change. **The cell is stated, the toolkit is used, and the decision proceeds.**

**Three signs the map is being over-applied.**

**Scenario analysis on a first-cell decision.** Which is effort without a corresponding risk.

**Bounding moves on a reversible commitment.** Which is friction without an exposure.

**The refusal, in a case where a calculation would settle the question.**

**Why the ordinary application deserves a section.** Because the framework's credibility depends on the cases it
excludes, and a reader who has only seen the serious examples will apply it everywhere. **The first cell is where
the map earns its right to be used in the fourth, and the earning happens through restraint rather than through
analysis.**

## The map and three neighbouring distinctions

The four cells are often confused with three neighbouring distinctions, and separating them keeps the map doing
its own work.

**Rare versus extreme.** Frequency is not the axis. A cell can contain frequent small events and rare large ones.
**The map's first axis concerns the shape of the tail, not the rarity of any particular outcome, which is why a
thin-tailed exposure can be catastrophic and a fat-tailed one can be quiet.**

**Uncertain versus unknowable.** Which is the interlude's distinction and belongs to the epistemology layer
rather than to the map. **A first-cell exposure can involve an unidentifiable quantity, and a fourth-cell exposure
can involve quantities that exist and are estimable.**

**Important versus payoff-dependent.** Stakes are not the second axis. The second axis asks whether the size of
the outcome enters the decision. **A high-stakes exposure whose decision does not depend on magnitude belongs in
the first or third cell.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is a distinction about a decision's stakes or its
knowledge, and the map's axes are about the distribution and the payoff. **Which is why the map cannot be used to
rank decisions by importance.**

**Why the confusions arise. One reason.** The four cells feel like a severity scale, and severity is what the
three neighbouring distinctions talk about. **Which is why the chapter's warning against reading a ranking into
the cells is repeated rather than made once.**

**How to keep the map separate. One sentence per axis.** The distribution's shape, and whether magnitude enters
the decision. **Two statements, and every neighbouring distinction is something else.**

**What the separation buys. One thing.** The map can be applied to small decisions without implying that they are
unimportant. **Which is what makes it usable as a filter rather than as an alarm.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The published text of the 2009 paper was not available to me. The description of the axes, the
contents of the quadrants, and the conclusions drawn from them rest on the author's own public
exposition of the same material, on the paper's abstract and citation record, and on secondary
discussion. Where the book quotes the paper's words, it says so; where it paraphrases, it is
paraphrasing an argument whose published form I could not read.

The check that the paper has no attached commentary was performed against the journal's indexed
records for 2009 and 2010. That is a strong check and not an absolute one: a commentary without a
registered DOI would not have appeared in it.

The special-section description in this chapter is based on the same record search, and the
companion papers are named there by author and page range.
